##### Transcript

###### The decline of civic ties

**0:00** · Hi, I'm Martin Felson. Welcome to City Design, the channel where we explore how we shape cities and how cities shape us.

**0:08** · Today's question is, how do cities improve our health and well-being?

**0:13** · Cities physically connect us. A first principle of city design is simple. We are not meant to be alone. We do much better when we share purpose in shared places. But today, our civic ties have thinned. Participation in clubs, associations, and congregations is way down. What's at stake isn't nostalgia.

**0:34** · It's social capital. The trust, the norms, and networks that help communities solve problems together. Why the decline in our physical connections, familiar forces, mobility uproots us, and screens capture our attention. As an urban designer, I also see an antidote.

###### The role of third places

**0:54** · Brick and mortar third places. These are gathering spots that are neither home nor work. They're where we swap ideas, organize, and belong. Cafes and barber shops, libraries and schools, faith halls and field houses. Third places normalize low stakes contact, and those weak ties add up to deliver enhanced well-being. They help us connect and cope together. Third places aren't new.

**1:22** · In the 1830s, Alexis Dtoqueville observed that Americans penchant for starting civic associations was a key factor to our unprecedented ability to make democracy work. He wrote that we're forever forming a thousand different kinds of associations, every kind, large and small. What happens inside third places? They convert bricks and mortar into trust and ties. Physical capital into social capital. Their design matters, too.

###### How spaces build social capital

**1:53** · Open, simple, yet versatile spaces instill a sense of ownership and group pride. Public libraries host book and hobby clubs, free classes, and meetups. Community centers host arts and fitness classes, neighborhood gatherings, and volunteer drives. Parks host walking groups, nature clubs, and community cleanups.

**2:18** · City service offices host neighborhood associations, and block clubs. Houses of worship host service groups, support circles, and food pantries. Parishes, JCC's, YMCA host wreck teams, community service projects, and family programming. Public schools host afterhour PTAs, youth clubs, and adult wreck leagues. Boys and girls clubs host teams, clubs, mentoring, and service projects.

**2:48** · Clinics and health centers host mindfulness groups, caregiver classes, and peer support. Food banks host nutrition and cooking classes, and volunteer and service clubs. Maker spaces host hobby clubs, and skill and repair shares. Museums, galleries, and cultural centers host dosan programs, lectures, and arts clubs. Rec centers host leagues, pickup games, and volunteer coaching and referee training.

**3:17** · Cafes and bars host book clubs, language tables, and interest group meetups.

**3:23** · Co-working spaces host professional associations. Farmers markets host info booths, volunteer signups, and community campaigns. Different places, same effect. Regular contact, small commitments, real purpose. That's how physical spaces compound into social capital and how social capital strengthens mental health and democratic life. Healthc care is catching up, too.

###### Policies for healthy cities

**3:50** · Doctors and clinicians now use social prescribing, which are patient referrals to groups, classes, and caregivers circles. Because joining a third place group measurably improves our health.

**4:03** · More broadly in the US, national public policies focus on jobs, families, and third places as direct paths to citizen and community well-being. Our industrial policy targets business sectors with incentives and penalties to raise job quantity and quality.

**4:21** · Stabilizes families with home ownership and good jobs. channels family members into community organizations to spur civic participation, which finally deepens civic trust and well-being through participation in third places abroad.

###### A third place first strategy

**4:40** · Some cities flip the order with a third place first strategy. Build third place social infrastructure. Catalyze networks of people and organizations that undergur local economies. Attract investment in jobs via quality of place.

**4:56** · stabilize family and home as civic life strengthens. Let's look at how this strategy works in practice. Polaris are small community centers cited across Mexico City. These are places to find free computers in internet, flexible classrooms, and hands-on workshops from carpentry to coding. Many include courtyards that flip from classes to festivals to civic meetings. Polaris work because sites are prioritized in underserved areas. Buildings are well-designed and easy to identify.

**5:29** · Programs are free and ongoing. In Ketal Kowal, this Polaris offers educational and practical support to rebuild social ties and safety within a dicey neighborhood. Classrooms and workshops open onto a shared courtyard and the operable facade signals that the space is open to all and available for everyday use and community ownership. In ease to Palapa on a tight site with little open space, the entry plaza and column threshold pulls the street inside the Polaris.

###### Case study: Polaris centers

**6:02** · Simple materials, strided block, concrete tile, steel create light, shade and durable rooms that flex from forum to classroom. In qui Quilo, a slender steel frame shades the interior spaces of this neighborhood hub. The inverted roof captures rainwater architecture doing double duty in a water stressed city. In La Pula, this educational center has a single unified room on two levels.

**6:31** · The large multi-purpose space offers free training workshops of all kinds for everyone in the neighborhood. In Valentine Gomez FAS, this Polaris is filled with naturally lit classrooms linked to a public walkway with lattice walls and gardens used for learning and neighborhood life. Free classes, workshops, and outdoor forums entice people of all ages to gather, learn, and belong. The bottom line here is that third places aren't a luxury.

###### Innovation in belonging

**7:01** · They're our everyday infrastructure of connection and well-being. Design them well. Program them predictably. Open them to everyone. The benefits compound.

**7:14** · We talk a lot about innovation in technology. Here's another kind.

**7:18** · Innovation in belonging. Cities that invest in it will be healthier, safer, and more confident about their future.

**7:26** · Thanks for watching City Design. If you're enjoying these episodes, please like, share, and subscribe.

Head over to Reactions to find out more about how they're celebrating Earth Day, and tell them Joe sent you! https://youtu.be/I1YLPfSuNXY

Most of the 600 billion pounds of waste that Americans produce every year ends up in landfills. All that trash can have huge impacts on the environment. But modern landfills have found a new use for all that trash — they’re turning it into energy. In spite of their reputation as “dumps,” these landfills are feats of engineering, more akin to construction sites. 

One of North America’s biggest landfills lies on the outskirts of Las Vegas. The Apex Landfill is not only one of the country’s largest, it’s also one of the busiest. Because it serves a non-stop city, the landfill must operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. It receives upwards of 16 million pounds of trash per day or 5 billion pounds per year.  

Landfills like Apex are required to deal with the toxic chemicals they produce, like methane, a greenhouse gas that’s 84 times more potent than carbon dioxide. At Apex, they capture that methane and turn it into energy that powers 11,000 homes in southern Nevada. 

Subscribe to PBS Terra! - https://bit.ly/3mOfd77

Hosted by Joe Hanson from It's Okay to be Smart, Overview uses incredible 4k drone footage to reveal the natural phenomena shaping our planet from a 10,000-foot view—literally.

**1:46** · trash dumped in piles with little regard for sanitation. As trash decays, it produces methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. We took a field trip to the largest green roof in New York City. Then we imagined what the city could be like if all of its roof space was green.

###### Intro

**0:01** · This is the largest green roof in New York City.

**0:04** · It's in the middle of bustling Manhattan, on top of the Javits Convention Center— a behemoth of a building with a six-block footprint.

**0:13** · But the roof hasn't always been green.

**0:16** · Before 2014, it was totally barren.

**0:20** · Now, just a few years later, when people walk out onto the roof, they say things like: "Amazing," "That's great," "I didn't expect this," "What a surprise."

**0:28** · But besides the great reactions, there are practical benefits.

**0:31** · We have 300,000 bees.

**0:34** · We've seen 25 different species of birds on the roof.

**0:36** · We reduced the temperature up here by about six degrees Fahrenheit.

**0:39** · And we also save about 7 million gallons of stormwater runoff that's absorbed in the soil and the plants that are on our roof.

**0:46** · We've been able to reduce our energy

consumption by about 26 percent, and that translated for us last year

into a saving of about 3 million dollars.

**0:55** · That is impressive.

###### Green Roofs

**0:58** · How does one green roof get so much done?

**1:01** · And what are all of the NOT green roofs in New York City doing with their lives?

**1:06** · First, let's see how much roof space actually exists.

**1:09** · You know, they are a major part of urban landscapes.

**1:12** · The the round number that most of us think exists is about 1 billion square feet.

**1:18** · One billion with a 'b.'

**1:20** · That's like 22 times the size of Central Park, in roofs.

**1:24** · And in most cities, what isn't roof is another impermeable surface like road, sidewalk, or parking

lot.

**1:31** · And these surfaces create a lot of problems for cities That green roofs can actually help solve.

###### stormwater runoff

**1:38** · Let's take a look at three of these issues. The first is

stormwater runoff.

**1:42** · Rainwater goes in pipes. It combines

with what's called sanitary water.

**1:48** · When there's too much rainwater, which happens hundreds of times a year around Manhattan, the wastewater treatment

systems shut down, and valves just let the water just,  you know, shunt out into the rivers. You know, it's got human sewage.

**2:01** · It's the biggest source of pathogens to

the Manhattan Island.

**2:04** · With green roofs, that water instead of going into the

drain and polluting the environment, ends up just evaporating the atmosphere

through the leaves of these plants.

###### heat island effect

**2:13** · And then, there's what scientists call the "heat island effect," which basically means that cities are significantly warmer than the surrounding areas.

**2:20** · I've seen asphalt roofs get up easily 170, 180 degrees Fahrenheit in the strong sunlight.

**2:26** · They absorb about 90 to 95 percent of the sunlight.

**2:30** · Green roofs, by comparison are close to air temperatures.

###### habitat loss

**2:34** · Another problem green roofs can help solve is habitat loss.

**2:37** · Cities can shrink or destroy the green space that's crucial for certain plants and

animals to survive.

**2:43** · Currently a lot of species might occur in  smaller parks throughout the city that are relatively unconnected, But having high densities of green roofs would allow those patches to be more connected.

**2:53** · Letting, for example, butterflies travel from patch to patch with lots of stepping stones of green roofs in between.

**2:59** · And these are just three of the problems that green roofs can help solve.

###### conclusion

**3:03** · But to really put a dent in any of these issues cities would have to implement green roofs at a large scale.

**3:09** · Stuart Gaffin, the research scientist

you heard from earlier, estimates that if all of New York City's 1 billion square feet of roof space were greened, those green roofs could lower the city's

temperature by nearly two degrees Fahrenheit and absorb over 10 billion

gallons of stormwater each year.

**3:27** · As cities continue to grow, all that empty roof space starts to look more and more like an opportunity, an untapped resource, a future ecosystem of problem-solving meadows in the sky.

We're destroying our environment at an alarming rate. But it doesn't need to be this way. Planet A explores the shift towards an eco-friendly world — and challenges our ideas about what dealing with climate change means. We look at the big and the small: What we can do and how the system needs to change. We'll take a truly global look at how to get us out of this mess.

#### How the US made affordable homes illegal

**Vox**, *08 16, 2021*

##### Video (9:41)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/0Flsg_mzG-M title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

The rules that keep American housing expensive.

Subscribe and turn on notifications (🔔) so you don't miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

Over the past year, housing prices in the US rose precipitously. Low interest rates and millennials’ entry into the market spiked demand across the nation, leading housing prices in some cities to increase by more than 20 percent in one year, and crushing the dreams of many would-be homeowners. 

But housing prices in the US were a problem long before 2020 — and while demand is a big part of the story, there’s an even bigger reason it’s increasingly difficult for Americans to find affordable housing: We don’t have enough houses. According to one estimate, the US is now facing a nearly four-million-home shortage. And the primary reason for that shortage is what’s called exclusionary zoning.

Zoning laws are the local rules and regulations that decide what types of homes can be built where. These rules can sometimes have good intentions. But they also have a dark history in the United States as a tool to keep certain races, religions, and nationalities out of white neighborhoods. And while zoning laws in the US are no longer explicitly racist, their effect remains basically the same: to keep affordable housing, and the people who need it, away from the wealthiest Americans.

Today, in the majority of the US, especially in cities with good jobs, it’s illegal to build many affordable types of housing. And it’s led to a widespread affordability crisis. Watch the video above for more.

Sources:

##### Transcript

###### NYC’s trash problem


**0:00** · Every year, New York City handles nearly three million tons of trash. For decades, mountains of garbage bags have lined the streets, feeding rats and blocking sidewalks.

**0:10** · Most people think that garbage goes up to solid waste heaven. It does quite the opposite.

**0:15** · Now, the Sanitation Department says it has a solution. Its trash revolution program aims to finally put a lid on the countless garbage bags piling city blocks.

**0:24** · But can redesigning the way New Yorkers throw out their trash solve a problem decades in the making?

**0:29** · We asked people who know the system best. Steven Cohen is the Director of the Sustainability Management Program at Columbia University, and he says one of New York's biggest solutions is surprisingly simple, changing how the city stores and collects its garbage. Instead of leaving flimsy trash bags on the sidewalk, the city's sanitation department is now moving towards sealed containers emptied by mechanized trucks.

###### Possible solutions


**0:55** · The motto of the Sanitation Department is New York's strongest. And now I think we're going to call them New York's smartest because they figured out a way to get the machine to do the work.

**1:04** · But changing how New York handles its garbage means undoing a system that's been in place for more than half a century.

###### Why the issue exists


**1:10** · We used to have metal cans that everybody had to put their garbage in that you would have to wash out after use. People in apartment buildings, superintendents didn't like doing that so much.

**1:21** · That's how New Yorkers put out their trash until the late 1960s. But when sanitation workers went on strike in 1968, residents switched to plastic garbage bags. And when the strike ended, the bags stayed.

**1:33** · This was really great news for the rats because it essentially created a buffet for them all over New York City of free food, because rats have no trouble at all getting into garbage bags.

**1:43** · More than 50 years later, trash bags are just as common as the vermin they attract, and the city's layout makes the problem even harder. Unlike other major American cities, Manhattan was built largely without alleys, leaving garbage with only one place to wait for pickup, the curb. The city is now trying to take those bags off the sidewalk altogether, replacing them with permanent containers like these.

###### What the sanitation department does now


**2:05** · The model that's used everywhere in the United States, either dumpsters in alleys, or 96 gallon sort of wheeled containers, wasn't feasible in New York City, because of our density and because of the way that our city's been built. So we looked to the model used in Europe, the stationary on-street containers, as the solution for a large number of our buildings.

**2:27** · Buildings can store trash in these bins throughout the week, and they all get emptied on pickup days.

**2:32** · You have a bin that's made of plastic, that's very durable, and there's a lot of garbage in that bin. And you have a mechanical arm picking up a tremendous amount of garbage and dumping it into the truck. The worker you see here is operating a machine and he doesn't have to go out and pick up the garbage himself.

**2:52** · And these bins seem to be working to keep out pests.

**2:55** · The pace is a little bit slower, but I think overall, I think for the community it's great. It does, we've seen the difference. I know they've been trying to tackle the rat situation, and it's definitely improved.

**3:06** · Businesses have been required to use closed bins since March 2024. And next year, the city plans to expand these residential containers to six more districts. By 2031, officials say New York City will be fully containerized.

**3:19** · This is a way to collect the garbage in a more efficient and frankly humane way, protecting the occupational health and safety of the workers. And I think this is really how robotics are changing all sorts of manual labor.

###### The bigger problem


**3:34** · In Cohen's vision for waste in the city, robotics would also play a larger role, sorting through the trash for recyclables to divert waste from landfills.

**3:42** · Humans do not want to spend their day sorting garbage. Robots could care less. And what AI can do is train those robots to really be able to identify what's coming past them. And as we get better at that, that waste stream suddenly becomes a trove of resources.

**4:02** · That could address a much larger challenge for New York. The city has nowhere to put most of its garbage.

**4:08** · The first place the waste goes in New York City is to a waste transfer station.

**4:12** · New York once relied on its own landfills, but as they filled up, the city gradually closed them. Fresh Kills, which was the largest landfill in the world at the time, closed in 2001.

**4:22** · We just ran out of space.

**4:24** · Today, New York's trash is offloaded at transfer stations, packed into shipping containers, and sent to landfills and waste-to-energy plants across the country. That process costs around $500 million per year. Waste-to-energy plants burn garbage to generate usable energy, offering an alternative to burying trash in landfills. But either way, the city still has to send its waste away.

**4:45** · In the map here, what you see is that, once we could no longer landfill in the five boroughs, we had to go outside the city. And you can see we go already 1,000 miles or longer to find a place to bring our garbage. We go wherever we can.

**5:05** · We're constantly looking.

**5:07** · That problem is only going to get worse.

**5:10** · We are going to be forced to ship our trash further and further, to places in the south and the Midwest where there's more space, there's more landfills, there's more capacity. And that's going to become really expensive.

**5:22** · Cohen's proposal could change that equation by reducing how much waste needs to be shipped out of the city in the first place.

**5:27** · The long-term vision I would have would be to build a waste processing plant that uses artificial intelligence and robotics to separate the useful resources and create separate places for those substances to be reused.

**5:46** · This concept already exists.

**5:48** · Materials processing facilities use automated systems to sort recyclables, but Cohen's proposal is more ambitious, applying that technology to New York's entire waste stream. Some tech companies are already experimenting with robots that can sort waste autonomously, separating out materials of all categories to be repurposed. In New York, Cohen says the technology would be economically transformative, using trash as a product to be sold rather than disposed of.

###### The bigger solution

**6:13** · The question is how a city as large as New York can implement this technology in the long term. The Sanitation Department has multiple programs in place for recycling and composting, but the technology is still developing. So as New York's trash disposal gets more expensive, recovering what's inside could become increasingly valuable. But making that vision a reality requires a lot more than just rethinking the city's trash collection.

**6:36** · Anything that isn't grown, anything that isn't organic is finite. And at a certain point, digging it out of the planet becomes more expensive than digging it out of your garbage.

#### How to turn your Neighborhood into a Village

**Andrew Millison**, *03 16, 2023*

##### Video (16:07)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/VoYZlyBHyQM title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Permaculture instructor Andrew Millison journeys to Portland, Oregon to talk with architect Mark Lakeman, founder of Communitecture Architecture and the City Repair Project. Mark initiated a movement in Portland to transform the homogenous neighborhoods of the city into places that have many of the qualities and characteristics that are found in some of the most treasured villages on Earth. Mark reveals the things you need to know to transform your own neighborhood into a village.

Mark Lakeman's architecture firm:

https://www.communitecture.net/

The City Repair Project:

https://cityrepair.org/

Special thanks to Maitreya Ecovillage in Eugene, Oregon for letting us film their sweet spot:

http://www.maitreya-ecovillage.org/

Andrew Millison’s links:

https://permaculturedesign.oregonstate.edu/

New York City is the most expensive place to rent in the United States, and some working class residents have come up with their own creative solution to the housing crunch: living out of RVs in quiet, industrial corners of the city.

The News Movement’s Dan Ming drove around the five boroughs, knocking on motorhome doors and meeting the people who make up NYC’s hidden network of RV dwellers.

#### Residential streets are too wide. Here's why

**City Beautiful**, *09 12, 2017*

##### Video (5:34)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/3g-z-PEzTas title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

In many places in the United States, residential streets were as wide as busy city streets. I understand why urban streets might need to be wide — parking, buses, traffic, and bike lanes all need the room. But why do quiet residential streets need to be so wide? Why do they need parking when all of the houses on the streets have garages and driveways? Why do they need wide lanes when most of the traffic is just cars and minivans? Why are we building residential streets as wide as big city streets?

Resources on this topic:

I based this video on my Master's thesis, which my advisor and I turned into a book chapter. You can buy the book, Retrofitting Sprawl, on Amazon:

#### Road diets designing a safer street

**Vox**, *07 19, 2018*

##### Video (5:14)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/Rs7jHvh7v-4 title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Reconfigure the lanes and the traffic will calm.

Subscribe to our channel!​ http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

Vox.com is a news website that helps you cut through the noise and understand what's really driving the events in the headlines. Check out​ http://www.vox.com​.

Watch our full video catalog:​ http://goo.gl/IZONyE Follow Vox on Facebook:​ http://goo.gl/U2g06o Or Twitter:​ ​http://goo.gl/XFrZ5H

Over the course of the 20th century, the car became America’s dominant mode of transportation. As vehicle miles travelled soared well past the rate of population growth, demands on the roadway surged. Congestion became a major issue. So transportation planners made the roads wider and added traffic lanes.

Today, we now know that bigger roads and extra traffic lanes do nothing to solve congestion. In fact, it tends to induce even more traffic. So we didn’t fix the congestion issues, and on top of that, we built wide roads that are relatively unsafe.

Transportation planners in the 21st century recognized that many of the roads that were overbuilt could be redesigned to calm speeding and add space for newer multimodal transportation options. And thus, the road diet was born.

The video above explains why road diets are implemented, and how planners survey the feasibility of a lane reconfiguration. You can learn more about road diets with the following resources:


https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/publications/research/safety/10053/10053.pdf 

https://safety.fhwa.dot.gov/road_diets/guidance/info_guide/rdig.pdf 

https://nacto.org/docs/usdg/conversion_of_four_lane_undivided_urban_roadways.pdf

##### Transcript

###### What is a road diet

**0:01** · This road might not look like anything special.

**0:03** · But what if I showed you the same road, a few years earlier —notice anything different?

**0:09** · Here’s a better angle of that: The old road has 4 lanes for traffic.

**0:17** · The new one has two.

**0:18** · And now there’s this middle lane for left hand turns.

**0:22** · There’s also a new bike lane.

**0:24** · This is what transportation planners call a road diet.

**0:28** · And it’s a very popular to make the roads safer.

###### History of overbuilt roads

**0:33** · Over the course of the 20th century, four lane roads became an American institution.

**0:37** · It started with the release of Ford’s model-T in 1908.

**0:42** · A few decades later, there was one car for every two households in the states.

**0:47** · By the 1960s, many roads became so busy, that traffic engineers had to figure out how to add capacity.

**0:54** · So, they added lanes.

**0:56** · A lot of pavement was getting put on the ground.

**1:00** · Even where maybe when the population and traffic volumes weren’t so high that we needed that pavement.

**1:09** · But we wanted that pavement.

**1:11** · Sometimes your eyes are bigger than your stomach.

###### Safety benefits

**1:14** · Fast forward to the present day and we’re left some overbuilt roads that are pretty unsafe.

**1:20** · And crash reduction is a major benefit that planners can achieve with just a bit a paint.

**1:26** · Four lane roads have quite a few conflict points -- these are places where accidents could happen.

**1:31** · These ones represent merging accidents.

**1:32** · These are rear ends, and there are multiple left turn crash scenarios.

**1:37** · Now look at what a 3 lane reconfiguration does — There are far fewer crash points.

**1:43** · A road diet can also make left turns suck way less.

**1:47** · The shared middle lane takes left turners out of the traffic flow, so they won’t hold up drivers who want to continue through.

**1:53** · And now, left turners will only have to cross 1 lane of traffic instead of 2, which will eliminate broadside accidents.

**2:00** · And the benefits don't end there.

###### Speed and multi-modal use

**2:03** · By slimming each lane in the road, the road diet reduced the travel speed by almost 7 miles per hour.

**2:09** · Narrower lanes can cause that psychological impact on the driver to slow down a bit.

**2:22** · And while a 6 mile an hour difference in speed may seem modest, it can make an auto accident much less deadly ... Narrower lanes also leave more space for expanded sidewalks or bike lanes.

**2:33** · your pedestrians will feel safer.

**2:34** · It might’ve given you more green space to separate from your vehicles.

**2:39** · And your bicyclists might have a dedicated space to ride.

**2:45** · In the midst of these changes, the number of traffic lanes has gone from 2 to 1.

###### Maintaining traffic flow

**2:50** · So if you drive a car, you might assume that the tradeoff of a road diet would be congestion...

**2:55** · How could traffic *not* increase?

**2:58** · That’s usually their concern before a road diet is implemented.

**3:03** · That’s not what happens.

**3:05** · The volume of the roadway is still sustained.

**3:08** · We wouldn’t want to put a 4 to 3 conversion on a piece of roadway that would then push half your traffic somewhere else.

**3:14** · And what we found in a couple of places, it actually makes moving through town easier.

**3:23** · But traffic flow is only one part of the equation — you’ve got to also balance commercial and safety benefits too.

**3:29** · especially if this is through an urban corridor where you’ve got businesses, coffeeshops, it works.

**3:34** · it keeps people moving, it doesn’t take traffic away from that corridor, and it reduces those rear-ends that thendo stop the road.

###### Contextual success rates

**3:45** · Iowa is conducting this road survey because so far, the plan has worked *really* well for them.

**3:49** · A study of 15 streets in the state saw a crash reduction rate of nearly 50%.

**3:53** · At the same time, the diet didn’t substantially disrupt other activities along their corridors.

**3:58** · A key factor was the traffic volume, measured by engineers as ‘Annual Average Daily Traffic’.

**4:05** · Most road diets will run into problems as you approach that 15,000 vehicles number.

**4:10** · In Iowa, many roads don’t get that much traffic.

**4:13** · The same could not be said for the suburban contexts in California.

**4:16** · A study comparing road diets in Iowa to corridors in California showed that California’s streets average about double the amount of daily traffic.

**4:25** · The same kinds of road diets resulted in a 17% crash rate reduction -- significantly lower than the reductions in Iowa.

**4:33** · This is not to say that the road diets in California are an outright failure.

**4:36** · It’s just a difference *context* for the road diet.

**4:39** · And the success of a road diet is driven by so many other factors -- economic impact, land use, or level of service to name a few.

**4:46** · What works in Iowa may not be the right fit for California, and vice versa.

**4:48** · So the case for road diets is pretty clear: they do slow streets down and they do reduce crashes.

###### Conclusion

**4:54** · But whether or not that’s worth the trouble depends very much on the context of the world that surrounds the road.

**0:01** · If you imagine a typical American city street, and you take away the space that’s dedicated to cars, you aren’t left with very much.

**0:09** · There are some narrow walkways on the side, and some bridges in between them, but not much else.

**0:13** · Cars dominate cities.

**0:16** · Spend some time walking around most cities and you’ll find yourself pushed to narrow sidewalks, waiting for crosswalk lights.

**0:20** · You’ll find cyclists navigating really narrow strips of space.

**0:23** · Americans are used to cars the way that fish are used to water.

**0:28** · That’s so ubiquitous in the U.S. that I think for most people, it just never occurred to them that it could be otherwise.

**0:35** · But what if there were a way to change that?

**0:36** · To give space back to pedestrians and bicyclists, and to make cities more friendly to life outside of a car?

**0:43** · It turns out Barcelona might have a solution.

**0:48** · In 2014, the city was faced with serious air pollution problems.

**0:51** · Barcelona and its 35 surrounding municipalities consistently failed to meet the EU’s air quality targets.

**0:57** · Studies were showing that air pollution in the region causes 3,500 premature deaths every year.

**1:03** · Traffic in the city also causes severe noise pollution.

**1:05** · So the city developed an extensive Urban Mobility Plan with the hope of reducing traffic by 21 percent.

**1:11** · The coolest part of the plan were these things: They call them "superilles".

**1:17** · Superilles?

**1:18** · “Si, superilles.”

**1:19** · That translates to “superblocks”.

**1:21** · It’s this urban design concept intended to minimize the presence of cars in city centers.

**1:26** · The word “superblock” has been used before to describe huge city blocks without any passageways for cars.

**1:31** · But that’s not what’s happening here.

**1:33** · So here’s how Barcelona’s plan works.

**1:35** · You take nine square city blocks and close off the inside to through traffic.

**1:39** · So buses, big freight trucks — or any vehicles that are trying to get from one part of town to the next — have to drive around the perimeter.

**1:47** · Inside the superblock, the speed limit is kept to 10 kilometers per hour — that translates to just over 6 miles per hour — and curbside parking is replaced by underground parking.

**1:55** · That means you wind up with street space for markets, outdoor games, and events.

**2:00** · Within this nine square block perimeter you're gonna have kind of a pleasant streetscape where people can walk around and mingle and do things without this kind of constant fear of cars around.

**2:13** · The concept is going to be tested out in five neighborhoods, but the city has identified 120 possible intersections throughout the region where it could be implemented.

**2:22** · So how do we know what the results of this kind of plan would look like?

**2:24** · Well, northwest of Barcelona is a city called Vitoria-Gasteiz, which has implemented superblock designs since 2008.

**2:30** · In the main superblock at the city center, pedestrian space increased from 45 percent of the total surface area to 74 percent.

**2:37** · With so much less traffic, noise levels dropped from 66.5 dBA to 61 dBA.

**2:43** · Most impressive of all, there was a 42% reduction in nitrogen oxide emissions and a 38% reduction in particle pollution in the area.

**2:51** · On top of that, business is up.

**2:52** · What you consistently see when people change their streetscapes to prioritize human beings over cars is you don't see any decline in economic activity, you see the opposite.

**3:03** · You get more people walking and cycling around more slowly, stopping more often patronizing businesses more, and that … center of social activity will tend to build on itself.

**3:15** · So here’s the question: could something like this work in an American city?

**3:20** · Barcelona has some unique advantages getting started on this plan, in that a lot of it was built before cars, and a lot of it was built on a simple grid.

**3:32** · The district of Eixample — where the superblock plan is based — was designed in 1859 in this repetitive grid structure by this guy, Ildefons Cerdá.

**3:41** · He basically invented the word for (and the study of) “urbanization” when he laid out this grid plan for Barcelona that evenly distributed resources like schools and hospitals.

**3:51** · But superblock designers insist that cities don’t need a simple grid structure to implement this kind of plan.

**3:56** · It can work anywhere.

**3:58** · Now, cities in the US have have attempted some car-minimizing projects like this.

**4:01** · The problem is, they’re usually done in wealthier areas with lots of existing businesses.

**4:07** · Zoning policies often require separation of residential and commercial areas — but an ideal walkable area would be a mix of the two.

**4:14** · On top of that, zoning minimums on parking availability encourage the presence of cars and parking lots, and minimums on street width make for wide, unwalkable streets.

**4:24** · Because of that, walkable districts are basically isolated luxury items in the US.

**4:29** · What makes the Barcelona plan different is that they aren’t setting aside one fancy neighborhood or town square to make pedestrian-friendly — instead, by proposing superblocks throughout the entire city, they’ve declared car-free spaces a right for everybody, no matter what part of town they're in.

**4:44** · Maybe — this might be overly optimistic — but I think it has sunk in in the U. S. that the model whereby every city resident comes with a car — and drives a car everywhere – is just inherently limited.

**4:57** · It limits the growth of your city, it limits the health of your city and the growth of your city.

**5:01** · So one way or another we have to find ways of having a lot of people live close to one another without all of them having cars.

**5:11** · You know, being able to get around and work and play in live and have enjoyable lives without cars.

Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

Starting in the late 20th century, modern streetcar proposals started rippling across municipalities in the United States. They’re touted as infrastructure carrying benefits ranging from the social to economic and the environmental. But these projects often make appearances in the news as costly, blunder-filled experiments in public policy.

Cities are willing to bet big on this technology for its potential to develop the local economy. But there is some disagreement as to whether the streetcar is driving this progress, or if it is simply the result of planning *around* the streetcar.

If you're looking for more information on public transportation and urban planning, here are a few links:

This interactive map by Yonah Freemark and Steven Vance allows you to zoom in on all public transportation projects across North America. http://www.thetransportpolitic.com/transitexplorer/#6/38.617/-78.673

This paper by Randal O'Toole of the CATO institute looks closely at the policy winds that drives streetcar proposals. https://www.cato.org/publications/policy-analysis/desire-named-streetcar-how-federal-subsidies-encourage-wasteful-local-transit-systems

For more information on New York City's streetcar proposal, you can check out the Friends of the BQX website here: http://www.bqx.nyc.

For a view of local opinions on the BQX, you can check out this documentary. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e8XmFjZOSSo&feature=youtu.be

New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo recently announced a plan to bring congestion pricing to New York City. The goal is to raise money for the city’s crumbling public transit system and reclaim the dangerously busy city streets. ###### Introducing congestion pricing

**1:17** · It’s called congestion pricing. And it means charging drivers for using the roads.

**1:21** · "Congestion pricing is an idea whose time has come. And I believe this is the year to actually get it done."

**1:31** · New York’s plan is still in the works, and it probably won’t be enacted until 2020.

**1:36** · But the end game is to reduce congestion by discouraging people from driving if they have other options like biking, or taking a train, or walking.

**1:44** · And to fund public transit at the same time.

**1:48** · It’s not a groundbreaking idea: congestion pricing is already old news in cities around the world.

###### The London model

**1:53** · London enacted a similar policy in 2003.

**1:56** · This is a necessary step for us to reclaim some of the space that is currently given to a motorized vehicles without ending up with gridlock.

**2:04** · Nicole Badstuber researches urban infrastructure and policy at the University of Cambridge and according to her, the system's pretty simple.

**2:12** · When drivers enter the Central London congestion zone between 7 a.m. and 6 p.m., they’re charged 11 pounds 50 pence – about 15 US dollars.

**2:21** · New York City's plan will be similar.

**2:22** · When drivers enter Midtown or Lower Manhattan, they'll face a fee.

**2:26** · There's cameras all around the roads at the edges of the congestion charging area.

**2:31** · They automatically recognize the name plate of the car or the vehicle entering the zone.

**2:36** · London has a few exemptions in place, like for people who live inside the congestion zone or vehicles with 9 or more seats and New York City will likely do that, too. And the system works.

**2:47** · So since it was introduced, we've seen that private vehicles entering the zone have gone down by 40 percent.

**2:54** · Overall vehicle traffic has gone down by 25 percent.

###### Results and public space

**2:57** · Cycling overall has increased 66% since the charge was instituted and bus ridership reached a 50-year high in 2011.

**3:04** · And wait times for buses decreased 25%, due to increased service both on buses and on the London Underground.

**3:10** · So we now, in comparison, still have much higher frequencies of London Underground services.

**3:15** · We can get more people, more capacity, more people into our trains because we have newer trains.

**3:20** · And like Nicole said, congestion pricing isn’t just about removing cars from specific zones, it’s about reclaiming a space for the public.

**3:28** · Picture Trafalgar Square, but designed for cars – an idea that was very much a reality before congestion pricing.

**3:35** · You would basically have a bus driving right past your nose as you come out of the National Gallery Reclaiming that section of road made the square safer and opened it to more public events.

**3:44** · No one could imagine going back to what it was before, and having these cars and buses zoom past you.

###### Resistance and future goals

**3:52** · London’s plan is widely embraced today, but it was met with resistance at first, with opponents arguing that congestion pricing could cut people off from health care, shopping, and schools.

**4:02** · Plus, people had to trust that the government would work efficiently and make significant improvements to their public transit system.

**4:09** · But within a year, London's congestion charging had majority support.

**4:13** · As New York’s plan is being finalized, some similar resistance is cropping up, which isn’t too surprising.

**4:19** · After all, it’s the first US city to implement this type of congestion pricing and no one wants to pay for something they’ve gotten for free for so long.

**4:27** · But the plan could generate up to a billion dollars for public transit, a system that most agree desperately needs repair.

**4:33** · And the city estimates it will reduce congestion by 8 to 13 percent and increase speeds by up to 9 percent, making a ride through midtown a lot easier.

**4:43** · So, like other cities where congestion pricing has been successful, it’s likely that people will end up accepting it.

###### Reimagining public roads

**4:49** · When we think of our roads, in particular in cities, as a sort of public good, as a public space, then if you're taking up more of it you should probably be paying for that privilege.

**5:01** · If you start to think about how everyone gets around the city, charging cars begins to make a lot more sense: You pay for parking, pay for the subway, pay to take a train or a bus, so why wouldn’t we pay for a city road?

#### Trains, planes and automobiles The state of U.S. infrastructure and why it's hard to build things

**Harvard Kennedy School**, *11 25, 2025*

##### Video (6:07)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/59IYXSv9218 title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

The state of U.S. infrastructure is improving, but not great, according to Samantha Silverberg MPP 2012, a former Biden administration official and visiting fellow at the Taubman Center for State and Local Government at Harvard Kennedy School. In this video, Silverberg discusses the challenges that face federal, state and local government officials who endeavor to fix the country's infrastructure, from roads and bridges to tap water and transmission lines. Topics covered include:

• The importance of infrastructure to our daily lives

• Why it's often challenging to get new infrastructure built

• What infrastructure priorities policymakers should focus on in the coming years.

You can read more about Ms. Silverberg's thoughts on our website: https://www.hks.harvard.edu/centers/taubman/state-and-local-perspectives/interview-samantha-silverberg-mpp-2012-taubman-center



About Harvard Kennedy School:

The John F. Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University is a graduate and professional school that brings together students, scholars, and practitioners who combine thought and action to make the world a better place.

Our mission is to improve public policy and public leadership across the United States and around the world so that people can lead safer, freer, and more prosperous lives. Harvard Kennedy School teaches current and future leaders the skills they need to effectively advance the public purpose in the public, nonprofit, and private sectors. Our renowned faculty and trailblazing research centers pioneer bold new ideas. And as the most international school at Harvard, we convene global leaders in the Forum, host visiting experts in the classroom, and attract a diverse community of faculty, students, and staff.

##### Transcript

###### The importance of infrastructure

**0:00** · Listen, right now it takes too long and it costs too much to build infrastructure in the United States, and we need to do something about that.

**0:10** · Infrastructure is so important for everything we do in our daily lives.

**0:15** · Think about the roads you drove on or the train that you took to get to school or work today, the tap you turned on and the water you drank, the internet that you use, even the electricity that powers everything in our homes.

**0:28** · But infrastructure is something that we really only pay attention to when it fails.

###### Current state and challenges

**0:33** · The state of infrastructure in the US right now is better than it was, but still not great.

**0:40** · The American Society of Civil Engineers gave US infrastructure a grade of C in its most recent infrastructure report card, and that's really because of decades of underinvestment in our infrastructure that has led to crumbling roads and bridges, unreliable transit systems, power networks that are unable to withstand the impacts of climate change and so much more.

**1:06** · There are tens of thousands of bridges in this country that are in poor condition.

**1:12** · There are millions of Americans that still don't have access to high-speed internet, which is far worse in rural America.

**1:20** · Our airports and ports lag their peers in other parts of the world, and the list goes on and on.

**1:27** · Infrastructure is funded and financed in a shared way through both the federal, state, and local government, primarily through taxes and user fees.

###### Funding and historical context

**1:38** · There are some privately-funded projects, particularly things like power plants or electricity transmission.

**1:44** · And then there are some that are a mix of private and public funding.

**1:48** · You can think of airports or ports or toll roads are often common examples of public-private partnerships.

**1:56** · Some of the most remarkable investments in infrastructure were accomplished by the United States government.

**2:03** · You could think about the Hoover Dam, the Bay Bridge, LaGuardia Airport.

**2:12** · These were all built during the New Deal.

**2:15** · When there was a real national effort that provided the resources, the trust, and the commitment of the entire American population behind what the government is doing.

**2:25** · I think there's a real and meaningful tension between efficiency and democracy.

###### Overcoming bureaucracy

**2:32** · When you want communities and the public to have a voice, which is a necessary and appropriate thing of any democratic process, there are often many veto points.

**2:43** · That process can be exploited by actors who are trying to stop good things from getting done.

**2:50** · The system right now is overly litigious.

**2:53** · Things like environmental permitting, which have an important and good purpose, have been used as a tool to stop good projects, even clean energy projects that have an overall positive benefit on the environment.

**3:05** · And as a result, these systems are getting in the way of progress.

**3:09** · If we want to get things done, we need to take a hard look at the way things are currently done within our governments and within our companies.

**3:17** · This means re-looking at rules and regulations and requirements that maybe each individually made sense, but when layered over years have created a process where well-intentioned public servants can't get anything done.

###### Investing in public capacity

**3:31** · The same time, we need to make sure that those public servants have the resources they need to do their jobs.

**3:37** · My colleague and friend Zach Liscow at Yale Law School has recently published research that shows how state departments of transportation have actually shrunk over time.

**3:47** · And those reduced staff have real impacts on the cost of projects.

**3:52** · Zach has shown that as staffs have declined, prices have gone up.

**3:57** · His team has also shown that experienced engineers actually save money on projects.

**4:03** · So if we're going to get things done, we need to invest in our public institutions, we need to invest in public servants, and we need to make sure that they have the tools to get their jobs done.

###### Successful projects and efforts

**4:13** · When we think about infrastructure projects, it's important to think of both the mega projects and the backyard projects because both of those types of projects have meaningful impacts on our communities.

**4:23** · On the mega project side, one of the examples that many people raise is the Mario Cuomo Bridge in New York.

**4:29** · This was the replacement of the Tappan Zee Bridge.

**4:31** · It was executed using an innovative procurement method at the time.

**4:36** · It also went through an expedited environmental permitting process, and as a result of both of those activities, it was delivered on time, on budget, and, by some estimates, saved billions of dollars for the taxpayer.

**4:49** · At the same time, I think it's really important to think about those smaller backyard projects.

**4:55** · In the Biden Administration, one of our priorities was to replace lead pipes.

**4:59** · There are still 9 million lead pipes serving our homes, which are a source of toxic chemicals.

**5:05** · Through money provided by the federal government, the city of Milwaukee has already replaced thousands of lead pipes.

###### Future priorities

**5:12** · I think the top three infrastructure priorities for the next 10 years are, number one, climate resilience.

**5:18** · We need to protect our communities from the impacts of climate change.

**5:21** · The second is clean energy generation and transmission so that we could power our future.

**5:26** · And the third is to close the digital divide, because we know that affordable, reliable high-speed internet is important for everything from remote school to work to accessing telehealth.

**5:37** · I also want to say, though, that every community knows what their own priorities are and they can't just be told by Washington where they need to invest.

**5:45** · And so the feds need to continue to invest in infrastructure carrying forward the legacy of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act so that our communities can invest in what they need.

#### Urban planners aim to eliminate slums—with a mathematical approach

**Science Magazine**, *08 29, 2018*

##### Video (2:49)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/YuRjeUkNf9o title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Researchers are testing a tool based on a "topological view" of cities and slums to improve the design of growing urban areas

Read the story:  https://scim.ag/2Nv8Gw1

Read the paper (free): http://advances.sciencemag.org/content/4/8/eaar4644


CREDITS

DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.1700362

photos and video

Luis Bettencourt and Christa Brelsford

Meagan Cantwell and Jessica Hubbard
 
script by

music

Nguyên Khoi Nguyên

##### Transcript

###### The role of city roads

**0:00** · What makes a city? People? Buildings?

**0:04** · Horrific traffic jams? That's not too far off.

**0:08** · It turns out that roads are what connect all the parts of a city.

**0:12** · We need easy paths to travel from place to place and for moving materials, supplies, and services.

**0:18** · And in some parts of cities—slums— that's not happening.

###### Infrastructure issues

**0:23** · The world's slums lack not only large, easy to travel roads, but they're also missing a lot of the infrastructure that goes along with them: street signs, building numbers, and vehicle access to building exteriors.

**0:35** · That lack of connectivity means that the billion people living in slums can't reliably get their mail, get to work, or even get to the hospital in an emergency.

**0:45** · Trash removal and sanitation are difficult at best.

**0:49** · Now, scientists are trying to transform slums with a mathematical approach to urban design called "topology".

###### Using topology for design

**0:56** · Slums can be broken down into two components: infrastructure, like homes and stores, and the access network that links them.

**1:05** · Nodes and connections.

**1:07** · With this framework, connections --in effect access-- can be optimized.

**1:13** · This new approaches already been used in two slums within Cape Town, South Africa.

###### Case study in Cape Town

**1:19** · In one of the two neighborhoods, most essential services provided by the city— water, toilets, electricity, trash removal— are on the outskirts where road access exists, but the inner portions of the settlement— where temples are—are completely cut off.

###### Mapping and optimization

**1:37** · In this study scientists used satellite data and detailed maps handmade by locals to diagram all the nodes and connections of the settlement.

**1:45** · They then used their topological algorithm to figure out which areas were inaccessible by roads, then generated the most cost effective ways to build roads and connect them to outside services.

**1:57** · In topology since one block of buildings surrounded by roads is considered equivalent, settlements with a wide range of shapes and sizes, from the suburbs of Las Vegas to the slums of Mumbai, can be analyzed in the same way.

###### Empowering local communities

**2:13** · The scientists who designed the program hope to come up with a user-friendly interface that can be used by communities around the world.

**2:19** · That, they say, would put the decision-making power into the hands of locals who can determine if proposed access roads will accommodate their priorities, then reroute them accordingly.

#### When Mold in the Home Is a Problem

##### Description

A first animated video in the 6-part Mold in the Home Video Series. It is an introduction to the series and explains when mold in the home rises to the level of a problem that must be addressed.

The Mold in the Home Video Series is created by the Environmental Health Investigations Branch of the California Department of Public Health. It is designed to answer basic questions about mold in the home using plain language in English and Spanish.

##### Transcript

###### Intro

**0:06** · Mold is in the air everywhere but you can't see it It is not an issue until mold in your home finds water and starts to grow.

**0:15** · Water can come into the home through roofing problems, plumbing leaks, bathroom moisture, and air gaps around windows and doors.

###### Signs of Mold Problem

**0:26** · You have a problem when mold appears near a leak or other dampness in the home.

**0:31** · Signs of a mold problem include the smell of mold.

**0:35** · Mold has a musty odor.

**0:38** · Sometimes you can't see the mold because it is hidden behind wall paper, dry wall, or paneling, or is on the underside of carpets.

**0:48** · The smell lets you know that it is an important problem.

**0:52** · If someone cleans or paints over the mold, it will return.

**0:56** · This is because the water problem causing mold to grow is not fixed.

###### Prevention of Mold

**1:04** · Mold is common around bathroom tiles, windows, showers, and sinks.

**1:09** · It can be hard to keep these damp places completely free of it But you can usually prevent this mold from growing by cleaning it regularly and increasing the air flow.

**1:21** · For more information, see the next videos in this series.

**1:25** · Visit the CA Department of Public Health's website cdph.ca.gov/Mold for information about mold in the home.

##### Transcript

**0:05** · Melbourne has been the most livable city in the world for the past seven years.

**0:09** · But this year it lost the top spot to Vienna.

**0:14** · Home to Strauss and Schubert and famous for its coffee houses, Vienna scored an almost perfect 99.1%.

**0:26** · But what makes a city livable?

**0:29** · The Economist intelligence unit has been analyzing this.

#### Why cities are full of uncomfortable benches

**Vox**, *11 29, 2017*

##### Video (3:59)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/WeyLEe1T0yo title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

That bench won't be yours forever.

Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

When designing urban spaces, city planners have many competing interests to balance. After all, cities are some of the most diverse places on the planet. They need to be built for a variety of needs.

In recent years, these competing interests have surfaced conflict over an unlikely interest: purposefully uncomfortable benches. 

Enter the New York City MTA. They’ve installed 'leaning bars’ to supplement traditional benches & save platform space. But designs like this carry an often invisible cost: they rob citizens of hospitable public space. And the people who experience this cost most directly are those experiencing homelessness.

A few notes of thanks:

First to Historian A. Roger Ekirch who kindly got me up to speed on the expansion of streetlights in historic western city districts.

Another thanks goes to author Veronica Harnish, who outlined some of the pitfalls that people experiencing homelessness face when choosing between sleeping rough or utilizing emergency shelters. You can read her blog here: http://car-living.blogspot.com/

A third thank you goes to the staff at the Unites States Interagency Council on Homelessness — they supplied the map in this video, as well as some aggregate statistics of the United States homeless population. Those numbers come from a variety of annual ‘Point-In-Time’ counts. The 2018 event will take place in late January, and the process depends on volunteers — so if you'd like to participate, you can find your local organizer here: https://www.hudexchange.info/grantees/find-a-grantee/?state=&program=on&coc=on¶ms=%7B%22limit%22%3A20%2C%22sort%22%3A%22%22%2C%22years%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22searchTerm%22%3A%22%22%2C%22dir%22%3A%22%22%2C%22grantees%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22state%22%3A%22%22%2C%22programs%22%3A%5B3%5D%2C%22coc%22%3Atrue%7D##granteeSearch 

Vox.com is a news website that helps you cut through the noise and understand what's really driving the events in the headlines. Check out http://www.vox.com to get up to speed on everything from Kurdistan to the Kim Kardashian app. 

Check out our full video catalog: http://goo.gl/IZONyE

Follow Vox on Twitter: http://goo.gl/XFrZ5H

Or on Facebook: http://goo.gl/U2g06o

##### Transcript

###### The problem with benches

**0:00** · Why are cities full of uncomfortable benches?

**0:06** · This one has armrests to prevent you from dozing off.

**0:09** · to prevent you from taking a nap.

**0:11** · Here’s another — again with the arms, the stiff metal.

**0:16** · And this one — it’s brand new.

**0:18** · The MTA in New York began installing them as part of a subway enhancement plan.

**0:23** · And they don’t call it a bench.

**0:25** · They prefer the term "leaning bars."

**0:28** · So what if i told you it was designed with discomfort in mind?

###### Defining defensive design

**0:34** · New York City is filled with some of the most innovative architecture and urban planning in the world.

**0:39** · Today, nearly every kind of public space here is has been developed with close attention to detail.

**0:45** · So these benches are no mistake.

**0:47** · They are designed to allow you to sit but not get too cozy.

**0:51** · And that is intentional.

**0:53** · The concept stems from a school of thought that goes by many names, but today we'll use "defensive design."

**1:00** · Defensive design is about moderating behavior.

**1:03** · The goal is to limit the ways an object can be misused.

**1:07** · These benches have armrests because that will prevent anyone from laying down.

**1:11** · Their short back is another nod to say, "This bench isn’t yours forever."

###### Examples of hostile design

**1:16** · This trend is worldwide.

**1:17** · And it’s not just in the benches.

**1:20** · When you start looking for defensive designs in New York City, you’ll find examples everywhere.

**1:25** · It’s the presence of security cameras in subway turnstiles or Times Square.

**1:31** · It’s these spikes on this column, meant to deter birds.

**1:34** · It’s the knobs on these ledges, to discourage skateboarders.

**1:38** · And there were once sprinklers underneath the awning of this bookstore, to prevent people from sleeping there.

**1:44** · It's sidewalk barriers.

**1:45** · It’s even these regular streetlights.

**1:48** · Streetlights are probably some of the most recognizable defensive designs.

**1:52** · When they surfaced in the 19th-century Western cities, the dynamic of urban life changed.

**1:58** · More people spent time outside at night, which drove economic development and a reduction in crime.

###### Controversy and impact

**2:04** · Most hostile architecture tries to influence behavior in a similar way.

**2:08** · The designs attempt to make public space a bit more hospitable, more ideal.

**2:13** · Defensive designs can deter crime.

**2:15** · It can prevent the destruction of public property.

**2:19** · And it can prevent loitering.

**2:21** · But there is a reason why defensive design is characterized as “hostile.”

**2:25** · Take the example of the bench again.

**2:30** · Disability advocates have a problem with that appearing in the MTA.

**2:33** · One advocate pointed out that "People who travel who have disabilities or just get tired sometimes need a bench to sit on, not a wall to lean against."

###### Targeting homelessness

**2:41** · And while no one likes an uncomfortable bench, these additions mean something more for people who are experiencing homelessness.

**2:49** · The United States is currently experiencing a decline in the overall homeless population.

**2:57** · But in New York, the homeless population is growing.

**3:01** · About 1800 people were found to have been sleeping in the subway.

**3:06** · That’s because emergency shelter isn’t always a viable option.

**3:13** · There are several examples of hostile architecture that target people who are homeless.

**3:18** · These designs imply that public space is not where homeless people should be.

**3:22** · As it goes, city planners have a dilemma — how do they design inclusive cities?

###### Designing inclusive cities

**3:29** · As for the enhanced subway initiative, the MTA’s mock designs highlight new USB ports and electronic signage in stations.

**3:36** · But you won’t find any press materials highlighting this uncomfortable bench.

**3:40** · Excuse me, the "leaning bar."

**3:42** · That’s because it makes for an uncomfortable discussion about who we design public space for — and who gets left out.

#### Why did we build high-rise public housing projects

**City Beautiful**, *10 17, 2017*

##### Video (6:48)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/7eGTU_uXLKk title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Watch this video ad-free on Nebula: https://nebula.tv/videos/city-beautiful-why-did-we-build-high-rise-public-housing-projects

In the spring of 2007, the Chicago Housing Authority demolished the last of the 28 buildings in the Robert Taylor Homes housing project. Robert Taylor Homes is one of several high profile housing project demolitions, from St. Louis’s Pruitt-Igoe to fellow Chicago project Cabrini Green. The demolitions serve as an admission that high-rise public housing wasn’t a good idea. The housing that replaced them are all low rise projects better integrated within existing neighborhoods. So why did anyone back then think it was a good idea? Why did housing authorities build these high rise projects in the first place?

Resources on this topic:

Hunt, D. B. (2001). What Went Wrong with Public Housing in Chicago? A History of the Robert Taylor Homes. Journal of the Illinois State Historical Society, 94(1), 96–123.

"Demolished: The End of Chicago's Public Housing" by David Eads and  Helga Salinas. https://apps.npr.org/lookatthis/posts/publichousing/

"When Public Housing Was Paradise" by Joy Connelly https://openingthewindow.com/2011/06/13/when-public-housing-was-paradise-2/

"Elizabeth Wood, 93, Innovator In Early Days of Public Housing" by Bruce Lambert http://www.nytimes.com/1993/01/17/us/elizabeth-wood-93-innovator-in-early-days-of-public-housing.html

"A Brief History of Public Housing" by Jennifer Amy Stoloff https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Jennifer_Stoloff/publication/228789405_A_brief_history_of_public_housing/links/5643a68008ae9f9c13e05df6/A-brief-history-of-public-housing.pdf

Video sources:
- Archive.org, Prelinger Archives

- Wikimedia Commons

Filmed in sunny Sacramento, California.

#### Why don’t we just burn our trash

**DW Planet A**, *08 13, 2021*

##### Video (10:45)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/OPVUrO-_7SM title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Waste to energy plants are seen as green innovations for countries where landfills dominate, as they reduce methane and generate renewable energy. But will these incinerators really make our trash problems go up in flames?

We're destroying our environment at an alarming rate. But it doesn't need to be this way. Our new channel Planet A explores the shift towards an eco-friendly world — and challenges our ideas about what dealing with climate change means. We look at the big and the small: What we can do and how the system needs to change. Every Friday we'll take a truly global look at how to get us out of this mess.

Open burning: https://theconversation.com/health-crisis-up-to-a-billion-tonnes-of-waste-potentially-burned-in-the-open-every-year-152778
